content: Otitis media refers to inflammation of the middle ear. It was first described by Hippocrates in the 5th century BCE. Early treatments were primarily surgical, with mastoidectomy being introduced by Jean-Louis Petit in the 17th century CE. The advent of antibiotics for otitis media began with the mass production of penicillin in 1940, thanks to Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain. The development of otitis media is closely linked to pathogens responsible for nasopharyngitis, including viral upper respiratory infections and bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Staphylococcus aureus. This fluid often contains the pathogens responsible for nasopharyngitis, triggering an inflammatory response. Otitis media can spread through respiratory droplets, saliva, mucus, or direct contact with contaminated individuals or surfaces. Genetic predisposition also plays a role, with evidence suggesting high heritability. Otitis media is classified into three main forms: acute otitis media (AOM), otitis media with effusion (OME), and chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM). Symptoms vary by classification but commonly include ear pain, a sensation of fullness in the ear, fluid discharge, and partial hearing loss. Acute otitis media often presents with fever, cough, and nasal discharge, while chronic otitis media with effusion may lead to neurological symptoms such as irritability, poor coordination, delayed speech development, and reduced attention span in children. Physical examination using an otoscope typically reveals erythema, bulging, cloudiness, and immobility of the tympanic membrane, along with the presence of effusion. Treatment for acute otitis media primarily involves antimicrobial therapy. High-dose amoxicillin is the first-line antibiotic, with alternatives like amoxicillin-clavulanate or intramuscular ceftriaxone reserved for cases unresponsive to initial treatment. Pain management includes acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or narcotic analgesics like codeine. Surgical intervention, such as myringotomy with or without tympanostomy tube insertion, is indicated for recurrent or chronic cases unresponsive to medical therapy. Tympanostomy tubes are used in cases of eustachian tube dysfunction or suppurative complications. For infants, breastfeeding for at least six months, avoiding pacifiers, and limiting daycare attendance can reduce risk. In high-risk children, prophylactic antibiotics may be considered. For chronic or recurrent otitis media, surgical interventions like tympanostomy tube placement can help prevent recurrence. The prognosis for otitis media is generally favorable. Acute otitis media often resolves within 14 days, while otitis media with effusion typically resolves within 3-6 months. Chronic suppurative otitis media may require surgical or prolonged antibiotic treatment. Complications, such as tympanic membrane damage or the spread of infection, can increase morbidity and worsen outcomes. The incidence of otitis media is high, with approximately 10% of the global population developing acute otitis media annually. Children under five years old are disproportionately affected, accounting for 51% of global AOM cases and 22.6% of CSOM cases. Certain ethnic groups, including Caucasians, Greenlandic populations, Southeast Asians, and Sub-Saharan West Africans, are more susceptible. In developing countries, factors like malnutrition, water contamination, and higher rates of HIV contribute to increased prevalence. Fatal cases are rare, with a case fatality rate of approximately 0.03%. Diagnosis of otitis media involves a thorough history and physical examination. Symptoms such as ear pain, fullness, fluid discharge, and hearing loss are key indicators. Otoscopic findings, including erythema, bulging, and immobility of the tympanic membrane, are diagnostic. Tympanometry can confirm fluid buildup. Imaging, such as CT or MRI, may be used to identify complications like mastoiditis or intracranial involvement. Laboratory findings are nonspecific but may show general markers of inflammation. In summary, otitis media is a common condition with a generally good prognosis when appropriately managed.
